title: Cellar safety: kegs, CO2 and gas
siteNotes: Where the cellar gas (CO2) alarm and its warning light or sounder are located, and what the alarm sounds like here
Who is trained and authorised to change CO2 cylinders and connect or disconnect kegs
Where the cellar ventilation switch or fan is and how to tell it is working
Where the safe place to gather is, and who raises the alarm and calls 999
Where the cellar emergency procedure and the CO2 risk assessment are kept
legalNotes: HSE (hse.gov.uk/coshh/basics/carbondioxide.htm), verified: CO2 is colourless and odourless and heavier than air. Effects as concentration rises include headaches, dizziness, confusion and loss of consciousness. Fatalities from asphyxiation have occurred when CO2 at high concentrations entered confined spaces such as cellars and displaced oxygen.

Workplace exposure limits for CO2 (EH40): 5,000 ppm (8-hour average) and 15,000 ppm (15-minute). Verified from the HSE page. Not used as slide figures, because staff do not need them; do not teach them to measure by feel.
COSHH 2002 requires an assessment of CO2 as a hazardous substance. Taken from search summaries: flagged as not read on the HSE site directly.

That a gas alarm should be fitted, what to do when it sounds (leave, do not re-enter, raise the alarm) and ventilation are good practice and common HSE and trade guidance. The HSE page fetched did not discuss alarms. Flagged. The trade guidance (BBPA) was not retrieved and the session does not quote air-change figures.

Cylinder changes only by trained people and kegs under pressure: Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000 and Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 are named in the session index. Specific rules were not verified here. Flagged.
The HSE pub cellar leaflet CAIS29 could not be retrieved: flagged.
Not verified: any specific fine or prosecution figure. None stated.

Review 6 Oct 2026: re-read hse.gov.uk/coshh/basics/carbondioxide.htm. Verified: colourless, odourless, heavier than air; headaches, dizziness, confusion, loss of consciousness; fatalities from asphyxiation in confined spaces including cellars; WELs 5,000 ppm (8 h) and 15,000 ppm (15 min). No wording changed. 'Never enter to rescue', 'leave and call 999' and 'ventilate only from outside' are standard HSE and trade rescue advice (a rescuer in a CO2 atmosphere is at the same risk) but are not quoted from an HSE page. A fixed gas alarm is a risk-assessment outcome rather than a stated legal requirement; the session does not say it is a legal requirement. GM or Ward Hadaway to confirm the cellar CO2 risk assessment exists and says whether an alarm is needed.

cards.title: Cellar safety: kegs, CO2 and gas
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- explain why a CO2 leak is deadly
- act correctly when the gas alarm sounds
- work safely with kegs and in the cellar

cards.title: CO2 can kill, and you can't smell it
cards.body:
CO2 is colourless and odourless, and heavier than air. A leak sinks and collects low down in a cellar, pushing out the oxygen you need.

HSE says deaths have occurred when CO2 entered confined spaces such as cellars. As levels rise you may get headaches, dizziness and confusion, then lose consciousness.

items.title: No smell
items.text: You cannot see or smell it

cards.title: If the gas alarm sounds
cards.body:
Treat every alarm as real. Your manager will show you where the alarm is and what it sounds like here.

Leave at once, warn others, and do not go back in. Never go in to rescue someone: a rescuer can collapse too. Call 999.

items.title: Leave
items.text: Get out and up to fresh air now

items.title: Warn
items.text: Tell everyone nearby; keep people out

items.title: Call
items.text: Raise the alarm; 999 if anyone is down

items.title: Stay out
items.text: Do not re-enter until declared safe

cards.title: Do not go in
cards.body:
If you suspect a leak, do not enter. Signs include the alarm sounding, a hissing noise, a colleague slumped inside, or feeling dizzy on the stairs.

Ventilate only if you can do it from outside and it is safe, for example by switching on the fan or opening an outside door. Do not breathe the air to check it.

left.title: Do
items: Stay out and raise the alarm

right.title: Do not
items: Go in to have a look
Reset the alarm and carry on

cards.title: Who changes the gas
cards.body:
Only trained, authorised people change CO2 cylinders or connect and disconnect gas lines. Your manager will show you who that is here.

If you are not authorised, do not try it, even if the gas has run out and the bar is busy. Tell a manager.

cards.title: Kegs are under pressure
cards.body:
A keg and the lines are under pressure. Disconnecting one the wrong way can release gas or beer with force. Only do what you have been trained to do, and release pressure as shown.

Kegs are heavy: use the right equipment and ask for help, as in the manual handling session.

cards.title: Ventilation and a tidy cellar
cards.body:
Good ventilation reduces the risk. Check it is on, and never block vents or switch the fan off. Keep floors clear and dry: wet floors, hoses and loose kegs cause slips and trips on stairs and in a tight space.

Report broken alarms, fans or lighting to your manager at once.

cards.title: A quick check, every time
cards.body: Before going down, check that the ventilation is working and the alarm is not sounding. Tell someone you are going in, and do not go alone without a plan. Your manager will show you the check-in plan.

items.title: Someone knows?
items.text: Tell a colleague you're going in

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- CO2 is odourless, heavier than air and can kill.
- Alarm sounds: leave, warn, call, do not go back in.
- Never enter to rescue someone.
- Only trained, authorised people change cylinders.
- Keep the cellar ventilated, tidy and checked before you go in.

cards.q: The cellar gas alarm sounds while a colleague is downstairs. What do you do?
options: Run down to bring them out
Take a deep breath and quickly go in
Raise the alarm, keep out and call 999
Switch off the alarm and see if it stops
cards.why: Going in to rescue puts a second person at risk. Raise the alarm, keep others out and call 999.

cards.q: You will smell a CO2 leak before it becomes dangerous.
cards.why: CO2 is colourless and odourless. The alarm and ventilation, not your nose, protect you.

cards.q: The CO2 cylinder is empty on a busy night and you are not trained to change it. What do you do?
options: Swap it quickly; it looks simple
Ask a colleague to hold the line while you swap it
Tell a manager so a trained person changes it
Disconnect it and leave the line open
cards.why: Only trained, authorised people change cylinders. Tell a manager and wait.

cards.q: Which TWO are right about CO2 in a cellar?
options: It rises and escapes through the ceiling
It is heavier than air and collects low down
It always gives a strong smell as a warning
It can displace oxygen in an enclosed space
It is harmless in small cellars
cards.why: It sinks and collects low down, and it can displace oxygen in confined spaces such as cellars.

cards.q: If you suspect a gas leak in the cellar, you should ventilate only if it is safe to do so from outside, and never go in.
cards.why: Stay out, raise the alarm and ventilate only from outside if safe. Never enter with a suspected leak.

cards.q: You smell nothing unusual in the cellar, but the gas alarm is sounding. What does that tell you?
options: It is a false alarm and can be ignored
CO2 has no smell, so treat it as real
The leak is only a small one
The ventilation has probably failed
cards.why: CO2 is odourless. Always treat the alarm as real and leave.

cards.q: It is safe to go into the cellar to check the leak if you hold your breath.
cards.why: Never enter with a suspected leak. You can collapse in seconds.

cards.q: What is the main risk when a keg is disconnected the wrong way?
options: The beer goes flat and is wasted
Pressure can throw out gas or beer
The line gets dirty and needs a clean
The keg gets lighter and is easier to move
cards.why: Kegs and lines are under pressure. Only do what you have been trained to do.

cards.q: A wet cellar floor and loose hoses are a slip and trip risk as well as a gas risk.
cards.why: Keep floors clear and dry. Cellars are tight spaces with steps.

cards.q: When should you check the cellar ventilation?
options: Only when the alarm sounds
Before going in, every single time
Once a week on the cleaning rota
Only on the days a delivery arrives
cards.why: Check that ventilation is on and the alarm is clear before every visit, and tell someone you are going in.
